beats: Hook: you can't copy a qubit (reuse line_cp_photocopier, the jammed copier; no-cloning is QC05-04), can't look at it without wrecking it (reuse line_qc_meas_flick_or_slap), and can't send it down a phone line. Yet with one shared entangled pair and two ordinary bits it arrives intact in another city. How?

Her story (Q25-07 53:00-56:42): make a Bell pair in the San Diego lab; the half called B travels to the San Francisco lab, the half called A stays (line_qc_tele_two_labs, line_qc_tele_case_handover; the pair comes from the pairing machine, reuse line_qc_pair_machine). The two cities are drawn generically: no landmarks, no signs.

In San Francisco a third qubit C holds the unknown state; a Bell measurement on B and C (the pairing machine run backwards, QC06-02) lights two lamps: two ordinary bits (line_qc_tele_bell_read; reuse line_qc_pair_machine_reverse; tape Q25-07 s49).

Only those two bits travel, by an ordinary call or letter, no faster than any call (clip Q25-07 55:47-56:13 'you are only sending classical information'; line_qc_tele_phone_call; reuse line_dials_daily_letter).

Four outcomes, four fixes: do nothing, X, Z, or both, and A is now exactly C's old state (58:19-62:55; tape Q24-08.notes p8; line_qc_tele_four_tools: an empty hook and three tools, the labels lettered on screen).

Her picture (clip Q25-07 57:36-58:02): B is a friend of A, goes to another place and finds a new friend C; A and C never meet, yet both are changed through B (line_qc_tele_friends). Quote her, never paraphrase into her mouth.

No cloning broken: C's state is gone in San Francisco the moment it is measured; one copy before, one after. Before the two bits arrive, A on its own gives 50/50 in every measurement, so nothing outruns light.
The first concrete use of entanglement (63:15-64:09). FACTS: Bennett et al. 1993; first experiments 1997. Keep to the textbook protocol and her two-lab story: no distance-record examples.

Measurement-based computing (64:15-65:10): entangle a big lattice of qubits first, then compute only by measuring them one by one; measured qubits drop out, so it runs one way (line_qc_mbqc_bead_lattice; Raussendorf & Briegel 2001). The Z-swap and X-swap circuits are teleportation shrunk to one qubit and a CNOT (65:28-70:29, tape Q25-07 s54).

Why photonics (67:19-68:37; clip 67:45-68:10): photons are cheap to make and easy to measure but barely interact, so gates between them are hard: make the entanglement up front, then measure (line_qc_mbqc_crossing_beams, line_qc_mbqc_optics_table); compiling for such machines (tape Q24-02 p11; OneQ, ISCA 2023: check authors and claims). Company names (68:10-68:37) stay off screen unless FACTS clears them; Q24-02 p12 has a third-party device image: do not tape it.

Cover (line_qc_cover_06_03; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): two benches far apart, the experimenter and the traveller on one long phone line, a matched cup at one end, two lamps at the other.
